The track crossed the stream only twice, at places where flat slabs of bedrock lay close to the surface and made a natural ford. Drovers bringing cattle south to the Ostley fairs widened the track in places by their passage alone. Hooves wore the softer ground into deep hollows, and in wet years these hollows ran with water and became small gullies that later builders had to fill.

The first deliberate construction came when the two towns agreed to share the cost of a cart road. The builders laid a bed of broken stone over the old track and edged it with larger blocks set on end. On the steep sections they cut the road into the hillside and built retaining walls of dry stone on the downhill side. These walls were laid without mortar. The stones were fitted so that each course leaned slightly inward against the slope, and rainwater passed freely through the gaps rather than building up behind the wall and pushing it outward. Many of these walls still stand, grown over with moss and fern, and the road surface they support has been raised and relaid several times above the original level.

The steepest part of the southern ascent is a series of eleven hairpin bends known as the Ladder. Here the road climbs nearly a thousand feet in under two miles of travel. Each bend was built on a platform of packed rubble wide enough for a team of four horses to turn without the rear wheels of the cart dropping off the edge. At the inside of each turn the builders set a stone post, worn smooth on one side by the hubs of wheels that scraped against it. In winter, snow collected in the angles of the bends and was cleared by hand with wooden shovels, the snow being thrown over the outer wall to fall down the slope.

The first inn on the climb was the Fallow Hart, at the foot of the Ladder. It was a long, low building of grey stone with a slate roof, set back from the road behind a cobbled yard. The ground floor held a kitchen, a public room with a broad hearth, and a row of stalls opening onto the yard. The upper floor, reached by an outside stair, held sleeping rooms with small windows set deep in the thick walls. Travellers going north rested here before the climb, and those coming south stopped to have their brakes and harness looked over. A smithy stood at the end of the yard. Its smith kept a supply of iron wheel-shoes, which were fitted under the rear wheels of carts to act as drags on the descent, and the scraping marks of these shoes can still be seen in places on the older stones of the Ladder.

Above the Ladder the road levels into a high valley of pasture called the Brennan Meadows. The second inn, the Lantern, stood at the centre of the meadows beside a spring. It took its name from an iron lamp that hung from a post at the roadside and was lit at dusk throughout the winter. In fog or falling snow the light could be seen from some distance across the open ground and gave travellers a fixed point to walk toward. The Lantern was built of timber on a stone foundation, which was unusual on the road. Its walls were of squared pine logs, notched at the corners and chinked with moss and clay. The roof was steep and covered in wooden shingles so that snow would slide off rather than settle and press down on the beams. The building had a deep porch where travellers knocked snow from their boots and cloaks before entering, and a drying room above the kitchen where wet clothes hung on poles in the rising warmth.

The highest point of the road is the saddle itself, a broad gap between two rocky summits. A small stone refuge stood here rather than a full inn. It was a single vaulted room with a hearth and a stone bench running around three walls. The vault was built of stone without any timber at all, so that it could not burn and would not rot. A keeper lived there during the colder months, kept the fire burning, and rang a bell at intervals during storms so that anyone caught on the open ground could find the door by sound. Beside the refuge stood a row of tall marker poles, painted red at the top, which traced the line of the road across the saddle. In heavy snow the road surface vanished entirely and the poles were the only guide.

The northern descent is shorter but steeper than the southern climb. The road drops through a series of rock cuttings into the gorge of the Tarn river. Here the builders blasted shelves into the cliff face and carried the road along them, with the river running fast and loud far below. Short timber galleries roofed several stretches of road where falling rock and winter avalanches were common. The galleries were open on the river side and backed against the cliff, and their roofs sloped outward so that snow and debris slid over them and dropped into the gorge.

The third inn, the Gorge House, stood on a ledge where the cliff stepped back to leave a small level space. It was a tall, narrow building of four storeys, built upward because there was no room to build outward. The stables occupied the ground floor, cut partly into the rock, and the animals' warmth rose through the floors above. The kitchen and public room were on the second floor, with a balcony that overhung the river. Water for the inn was drawn up from a channel cut into the rock face above, which caught a stream before it fell into the gorge and carried it to a stone cistern behind the kitchen.

The road and its inns changed slowly over the centuries. The surface was paved with fitted setts on the steeper sections so that horses would have better footing. Drainage culverts of shaped stone were laid beneath the road at intervals to carry stream water across without washing out the surface. Later, when wheeled coaches began to run a regular service between the two towns, the inns added coach houses and more sleeping rooms. The Fallow Hart gained a second wing. The Lantern was rebuilt in stone after a fire, though its builders kept the steep roof and the deep porch of the old timber house.

# The Weather of Brackenhowe Moor

Brackenhowe Moor is a broad upland plateau of blanket bog, heather and coarse grass that rises gently from the valley farms on its eastern side and ends abruptly in a line of gritstone edges facing west. Its highest ground is a low, rounded summit called Carl Knott, marked by a cairn and an old boundary stone. Streams drain the moor in shallow peat channels that deepen into steep wooded cloughs as they fall toward the lowlands. Because the plateau faces the prevailing westerly winds with almost nothing to break them, its weather is wetter, windier and colder than that of the valleys a short distance below. The moor's year follows a recognisable sequence, although any given season may arrive early, linger or briefly reverse.

Winter on Brackenhowe begins in late November, when the low sun no longer warms the peat by day and the ground holds the night's cold. The dominant weather comes from the Atlantic in a procession of depressions, each bringing a warm, damp airstream ahead of it and a colder, gusting one behind. As moist air is driven up the western edges it cools, and its water vapour condenses into cloud that settles directly onto the plateau. On many winter days the summit stands inside this cloud from dawn to dusk, and the moor is reduced to a grey space a few dozen paces across, in which rain and drizzle seem to drift sideways rather than fall. The wind on the open top commonly blows hard enough to lean a walker forward, and in the strongest gales it lifts standing water off the bog pools and carries it away as spray.

Snow falls when the air behind a depression is cold enough or when a continental airstream arrives from the east. Easterly snow tends to be fine and dry and comes with a hard, steady wind that sweeps it from the exposed heather and packs it into the lee of every bank, wall and peat hag. After such a fall the plateau shows a striped pattern of bare dark ground and long white drifts, and the gullies on the eastern cloughs may fill level with their banks. Westerly snow is usually wetter and heavier, clinging to fence posts and the windward faces of the gritstone. On still nights after snow the air above the moor becomes very clear, and the snow surface loses heat to the sky, so that the coldest air gathers in the hollows and slides downhill into the cloughs. By morning a thick hoar frost may cover the rushes, and the wire fences carry feathered ice crystals that grow outward into the wind that brought the moisture.

Rime ice is a particular feature of the summit in winter. When supercooled cloud droplets meet the cairn, the boundary stone or the old iron posts along the parish line, they freeze on contact and build up layers of white ice that extend toward the wind. Over several days of freezing fog these deposits can grow into flat plumes as long as a forearm. A change to a mild westerly brings thaw, and the rime breaks away in pieces that litter the ground around the cairn. Thaw on Brackenhowe is often abrupt. Warm rain falling on lying snow releases the water held in both, and the frozen peat beneath cannot absorb it, so the streams rise quickly and run brown and loud through the cloughs.

Spring arrives late on the plateau and in uneven stages. March often brings bright, cold days with showers of hail or sleet that blow across the moor as distinct dark columns, each one followed by sunshine on wet heather. The ground remains cold, and late snow is common into April, though it rarely lasts more than a day or two on the open moor. As the sun climbs higher, the dark peat surface begins to absorb more of its warmth, and on calm afternoons the air above the bog shimmers faintly. Curlews and golden plover return as the frosts weaken, and the cotton grass flowers in the wetter hollows, its white heads appearing in late April and May. In this season the moor sometimes lies above a sea of valley fog. Cool, damp air settles in the lowlands overnight, while the plateau stands in clear air with a view across a flat white surface broken only by distant hilltops.

Drier spells become more frequent toward late spring, when high pressure settles over the region for days at a time. Under these conditions the wind falls light, the sky is pale blue and the upper layers of peat begin to dry and crack. The sphagnum mosses in the pools hold their water, but the drier hummocks and the exposed peat on the edges turn pale and crumbling. Brackenhowe has a long history of spring fires during such spells, some started by lightning but most by people, and old burn scars can still be traced across the eastern slopes as patches of younger heather of a uniform height.

Summer on the moor is milder than in the valleys and rarely hot. Even on warm days a breeze crosses the plateau, and its temperature drops noticeably on the summit compared with the farms below. Cumulus clouds form over the moor on sunny mornings as the ground warms and rising air carries moisture upward. These clouds often grow larger over the high ground than over the surrounding country, and on some afternoons they build into towering thunderstorms. Storms over Brackenhowe tend to arrive from the south or south-west, preceded by a heavy stillness and a darkening of the light over the edges. When they break, rain falls with great intensity for a short time, and lightning frequently strikes the higher ground. Downpours of this kind cannot soak into dry peat fast enough, and water runs off in sheets, cutting fresh channels in bare ground and carrying dark sediment into the streams.

In August the heather flowers and the moor turns a deep purple that is visible from the valleys. The air in late summer is often hazy, and the long views of spring give way to softened outlines. Mist returns more often as the month ends, especially in the early mornings, when cooled air condenses into low cloud that clings to the plateau until the sun burns it away by late morning.

Autumn on Brackenhowe is marked by the return of the Atlantic depressions in strength. September may bring settled, golden days with dew heavy on the grass and spider webs visible across the heather, but the first major gales usually arrive by October. The bracken on the lower slopes turns rust brown, and the cotton grass and moor grasses fade to straw. Rainfall increases, the bog pools fill, and the streams that dwindled in summer flow strongly again. The cloud base drops, and the summit spends more of its days hidden. Frost returns to the hollows in clear, calm nights, at first only lightly and then more sharply as the weeks pass.

# The Wendle and Ashcombe Canal

The Wendle and Ashcombe Canal is a narrow inland waterway in the fictional county of Breckshire. It runs for thirty-one miles from the tidal basin at Wendle Quay, on the estuary of the River Saur, to the market town of Ashcombe in the limestone uplands to the north-east. Along its course it rises nearly four hundred feet through thirty-four locks, crosses two river valleys on aqueducts, and passes beneath Callow Ridge through a tunnel a little over a mile long. For most of its working life it carried coal, lime, grain, timber and building stone. Today it carries mainly pleasure craft, along with a small number of residential boats moored near its two terminal towns.

The canal was cut between 1789 and 1802 by gangs of labourers working with picks, shovels and wheelbarrows. The engineer laid out the line to follow the contours of the land wherever possible, so that long level stretches, called pounds, could run without locks. Where the ground rose too steeply for the channel to follow it, the locks were grouped together into flights. The largest of these is the Thornholt Flight, eleven locks set close together on the southern face of Callow Ridge, where the canal climbs nearly a hundred and twenty feet in less than a mile. Elsewhere the locks stand alone or in pairs, separated by pounds that sometimes run for several miles.

The bed and banks of the canal were sealed with puddled clay. Workers prepared this material by kneading wet clay with spades and by driving cattle back and forth through it until it formed a dense, watertight paste. They laid the puddle in layers along the bottom and sides of the channel and trod each layer firm before adding the next. The finished channel is about thirty feet wide at the water surface and about five feet deep at the centre, narrowing to shallow shelves at the edges. A towpath, surfaced with cinders and later with gravel, runs along one bank for the whole length of the canal. It changes sides at several points, and at each of these a turnover bridge allows a horse to cross without being unhitched from its boat.

Each lock on the Wendle and Ashcombe is a rectangular chamber of brick and dressed stone, slightly more than seventy feet long and seven feet wide. Every chamber is closed by a pair of mitred gates at its lower end and a single gate at its upper end. The gates are built of oak, with heavy balance beams projecting over the lockside. A person working the lock pushes against the beam to swing the gate open or shut. Set into each gate, or into culverts in the chamber walls, are sluices known locally as paddles. These are wooden shutters raised and lowered by a rack and pinion, which is turned with a detachable iron windlass.

The operation of a lock relies entirely on gravity. To raise a boat, the lower gates are opened while the chamber stands at the level of the lower pound, and the boat enters. The lower gates are then closed and the upper paddles drawn. Water from the higher pound flows into the chamber and lifts the boat until the levels inside and outside the upper gate are equal. The upper gate can then be pushed open, and the boat leaves. Lowering a boat reverses the sequence, with water released through the lower paddles into the pound below. The mitred lower gates meet at an angle that points upstream, so the weight of water in a full chamber presses them firmly together and holds them closed.

Every passage through a lock draws a chamberful of water from the summit downward, and the canal needs a constant supply to replace it. The summit pound, which runs for six miles across the plateau above Callow Ridge, is fed by two reservoirs. Hesketh Water lies in a shallow valley to the west and was formed by an earth dam with a clay core. Linnet Pool is smaller and lies to the east, held back by a masonry wall. Feeder channels carry water from both reservoirs into the summit. At intervals along the canal, overflow weirs let surplus water spill into side streams so that the pounds do not overtop their banks during heavy rain.

The Callow Tunnel was the most difficult work on the whole line. Its builders sank a series of vertical shafts from the hilltop along the line of the tunnel. At the bottom of each shaft, gangs dug outward in both directions until the separate headings met. The tunnel is lined with brick and is just wide enough for a single narrow boat. It has no towpath. In the early decades, boats were taken through by legging. Two men lay on their backs on boards that projected from either side of the bow and walked their feet along the tunnel walls, pushing the boat forward while the horse was led over the top of the ridge along a path still called the Horse Road. The ventilation shafts remain open above the tunnel, capped with iron grilles, and their brick rims stand in the fields like low chimneys.

The boats that worked the canal were narrow boats, built to fit the locks with only a few inches to spare. A typical boat was about seventy feet long and just under seven feet wide. It had a flat bottom, upright sides and a hold that took up most of its length. The earliest boats were built of elm and oak planking on oak frames. Their holds were open to the weather, though they could be covered with tarpaulin sheets stretched over a light ridge of planks and stanchions. At the stern was a small cabin, about ten feet long, where the boatman and often his family lived. The cabin held a coal range, a fold-down table, a side bed and a cross bed, all fitted into a space barely taller than a standing adult. The interiors were painted with roses, castles and geometric borders, and the exteriors carried the owner's name in shaded lettering.

For its first sixty years the canal was worked by horse-drawn boats. A single horse could pull a loaded boat of around twenty-five tons at a steady walking pace, and the towline ran from a mast near the bow to the horse's harness on the towpath. Stables stood beside many of the locks and at the wharves, along with small cottages for the lock keepers. At Wendle Quay a covered transhipment shed was built over a side basin. There, cargoes were moved between the narrow boats and the broader sailing barges that worked the estuary. Ashcombe had a long open wharf lined with lime kilns, coal yards and a granary of five storeys with a projecting hoist.

In the second half of the nineteenth century, a railway was opened along the valley of the Saur, and long-distance traffic on the canal began to fall away. Coal and lime from the uplands now went by rail, and the canal company reduced its tolls to keep the local trade. Some boats were converted to carry roadstone and manure, and several of the smaller wharves fell out of use. Around the turn of the century the first steam-powered boats appeared on the canal. These were wooden hulls fitted with small boilers and single-cylinder engines turning a propeller. A steamer could tow one or two unpowered boats, called butties, behind it. Steam towing tugs were also stationed at both ends of the Callow Tunnel, and they replaced legging altogether.

In the decades that followed, steam gave way to internal combustion. Boats were fitted with single- and twin-cylinder diesel engines, which took up much less room than a boiler and needed no stoker. Hulls began to be built of riveted iron, and later of welded steel, while the cabin layout of the wooden boats was kept largely unchanged. The paired working of a motor boat and a butty became the usual arrangement for the remaining trade. The motor boat steered from the stern, and the butty followed on a short line, its own tiller worked by a second member of the crew.

Commercial carrying ended on the upper half of the canal shortly after the middle of the twentieth century, when the last regular coal contract to Ashcombe was lost. Over the next twenty years the locks of the Thornholt Flight decayed. Their gates rotted in place, reeds spread across the summit pound, and a section of the bank near Hesketh Water collapsed, draining the pound into the fields below. The lower canal stayed in water and was used by a few maintenance craft and by fishermen.

The restoration of the canal was carried out in stages over several decades. New oak gates were made and hung, the collapsed bank was rebuilt with a concrete core, and the reservoirs were cleared of silt. The tunnel lining was repointed and in places rebuilt, and a one-way traffic system was put in place, controlled by signals at each portal. The Thornholt Flight reopened last, and with it the full length of the canal became navigable again.
